title: Cut coding agent costs by 90%: Secure LLM serving with Ray + vLLM on Anyscale
gist: Anyscale argues that teams can self-host open-weight coding models on Ray Serve LLM + vLLM for a projected $17-58 per developer per month versus roughly $800/month of equivalent Claude Code API spend, and documents the measured tuning knobs (CUDA graphs, MTP, KV offload, cache-aware routing). It is a vendor guide with explicit caveats that cost figures are planning projections, not TCO.

insights.claim: Anyscale's cost model projects self-hosted serving at about $2,920 per month always-on (about $58 per registered developer) or about $840 per month for work hours only (about $17 per developer), assuming roughly $4 per GPU-node hour for an RTX PRO 6000 and 50 registered developers sharing one GPU.
insights.speaker: Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Headline claim of up to 90% savings rests on a 50-developer-per-GPU assumption that must be validated on real traces.

insights.claim: An active developer routinely runs up about $800 per month in equivalent Claude Code API costs, roughly $40,000 and 171M output tokens per month for a 50-developer team.
insights.speaker: Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Per-token API spend scales linearly with developers while shared GPUs offer scale efficiencies.
insights.locator: An active developer routinely runs up about $800

insights.claim: Coding-agent workloads are heavily input-skewed: the WekaTrace dataset shows a 117:1 input-to-output token ratio and SyFI TraceLab's Claude trace shows 269:1 with a 95.2% prompt cache hit rate.
insights.speaker: Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Prefill and caching, not decode, dominate cost and latency in agentic coding.

insights.claim: BMW found the cost-benefit of moving from API to in-house inference with as few as 8 developers.
insights.speaker: Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: A named enterprise reference point for the break-even team size.
insights.quote: BMW found the cost-benefit of moving from API to in-house inference with as few as 8 developers.

insights.claim: The authors caution that per-developer GPU costs are planning projections, not total cost of ownership, because decode tests ignore prefill, queuing, utilization, latency SLOs and model quality; real savings need sustained trace-replay goodput and platform operations overhead.
insights.speaker: Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Treat the 90% figure as an upper-bound marketing headline until measured.

themes.theme: Why self-host: control, privacy and data flywheel

insights.claim: Coding agents send source code, internal docs and architecture decisions to the model on every request, so owning the runtime keeps code, traces and usage data inside the perimeter and enables later post-training on that data.
insights.speaker: Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Data control is positioned as a second driver beyond cost for in-house inference.
insights.locator: Coding agents repeatedly send repository context

insights.claim: Hosting open-weight models also reduces dependence on one provider's rate limits and lock-in, and enables a flywheel of capturing approved agent traces, curating them with Ray Data and post-training with Ray Train or an RL framework.
insights.speaker: Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Open-weight stacks turn usage into proprietary training data.
insights.locator: Hosting an open-weight model on Anyscale

insights.claim: Coinbase post-trained Qwen3.5-9B with SkyRL on proprietary fraud data for its Onramp fraud agent; the model outperformed Claude Opus 4.5 on all four fraud-detection metrics and cut end-to-end serving latency by 55%.
insights.speaker: Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Evidence that small post-trained open models can beat frontier models on narrow domain tasks.

insights.claim: Coding-agent prompts combine system instructions, repository context, tool definitions and history to produce often a short edit, making the workload prefill-heavy with large inputs dominating TTFT and strong opportunity for prefix KV-cache reuse.
insights.speaker: Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Infrastructure should be tuned for prefix reuse rather than raw decode throughput.

insights.claim: The stack splits into vLLM as inference engine, Ray Serve LLM for scaling, routing and OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible endpoints, and the Anyscale platform for GPU provisioning, autoscaling with scale-to-zero and observability.
insights.speaker: Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Defines the layered build-versus-buy boundary for self-hosted inference.
insights.locator: How the LLM serving stack operates

insights.claim: Claude Code, Codex and Cursor can be pointed at a custom endpoint via /v1/messages, /v1/responses and /v1/chat/completions respectively, so one service can serve all three harnesses.
insights.speaker: Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Client lock-in is weak: major coding harnesses accept custom model endpoints.

insights.claim: A Ray Serve LLM benchmark reported cumulative throughput gains of up to 4.4x on prefill-heavy and 24.8x on decode-heavy workloads versus an older unbatched baseline after HAProxy, direct streaming and RayExecutorV2.
insights.speaker: Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Vendor-reported framework gains relative to a weak baseline.
insights.locator: A published recent Ray Serve LLM benchmark

insights.claim: Models should be chosen on task success, not leaderboard rank, by measuring cost per successful task rather than cost per million tokens, since a smaller model finishing in one turn can be cheaper than a larger one needing more GPUs.
insights.speaker: Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Unit economics of agents hinge on retries and turns, not token price.
insights.quote: Measure cost per successful task, not only cost per million tokens.

insights.claim: Benchmark scores often reflect the full agent system rather than the model alone, so results are comparable only when benchmark versions and evaluation setups match.
insights.speaker: Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Public agent leaderboards are weak procurement signals.

insights.claim: NVFP4 on Blackwell halves raw storage versus FP8, but the tested Qwen checkpoint used about 22 GB versus 27 GB for FP8, a 19% reduction, and on RTX PRO 6000 the pinned vLLM release uses a Marlin fallback and an FP8 KV cache.
insights.speaker: Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Real-world quantization savings and kernel support lag headline numbers.

insights.claim: FP8 KV cache fits about 6.53x 256K-token contexts versus 3.27x with BF16 on the tested 96 GB GPU.
insights.speaker: Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: KV quantization doubles concurrent long-context capacity.
insights.locator: Quantize the KV cache when supported

insights.claim: Single-GPU gains from CUDA graphs (15.9 to 45.6 output tokens/s, 2.87x), multi-token prediction (65 to 121 tokens/s, 1.86x), RunAI Streamer weight loading (about 85 s to 25 s) and restored compile cache (48.5 s to 6.0 s, 8.0x) are measured per knob and are not cumulative.
insights.speaker: Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Each knob is independently valuable but total speedup cannot be multiplied.

insights.claim: Higher speculative depth is not inherently better: at concurrency 8, three predicted tokens gave 99 tokens/s versus 80 for two and 74 for four, and upstream issues note corrupted tool calls when combining MTP with prefix caching.
insights.speaker: Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Speculative decoding must be regression-tested for tool-call correctness before production.
insights.locator: Test speculative decoding against target workloads

insights.claim: The recommended order is correct tool use with speculation off, then quantization and context length, CUDA graphs, chunked prefill tuning, speculative decoding, and finally cold-start optimization, rerunning correctness and load tests.
insights.speaker: Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: A practical sequencing playbook for tuning inference.
insights.locator: In practice, first establish correct tool use

insights.claim: Benchmarks should replay real agent sessions, such as converted Claude Code JSONL sessions or the WekaTrace corpus, and optimize goodput (share of requests meeting latency SLOs) instead of raw throughput, since uniform synthetic prompts miss repeated prefixes and heavy-tailed sessions.
insights.speaker: Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Synthetic benchmarks overstate capacity for agent traffic.
insights.quote: Uniform synthetic prompts fail to capture a true agent loop.
insights.locator: Replay real agent sessions for benchmarks

insights.claim: A 512 GiB CPU KV-cache tier on a GLM-5.2 8x RTX PRO 6000 node raised request throughput 3.79x (0.0625 to 0.2367 req/s), lifted the cached prompt-token share from 6.1% to 74.9% and cut median TTFT from 48.4 s to 9.2 s.
insights.speaker: Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Offloading idle sessions to CPU memory makes long-lived coding sessions economical.
insights.locator: In an internal benchmark on a GLM-5.2 workload

insights.claim: Autoscaling should be sized as roughly (256K / 85K) x 20 = 60 concurrent requests as the admission ceiling, with target_ongoing_requests set 20-30% lower, and distinct vLLM max_num_seqs, Ray Serve max_ongoing_requests and autoscaling targets.
insights.speaker: Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete capacity-planning formula for long-context agent traffic.

insights.claim: Ray Serve LLM's KVAwareRouter scores replicas by remaining prefill plus active prefill and ongoing decode, but it is currently compatible only with Codex; other clients should use consistent hashing for session affinity.
insights.speaker: Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Cache-aware routing support is uneven across coding clients.

insights.claim: A CPU-only LiteLLM gateway can route simple requests to Qwen, intermediate tasks to GLM and complex reasoning or multimodal work to Claude, with session stickiness so tool-result steps do not switch models mid-session.
insights.speaker: Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Hybrid routing captures most savings while retaining frontier quality where needed.
insights.locator: In our internal setup, the gateway routes

insights.claim: Three multi-model routing policies are route by task complexity, fall back to hosted models when self-hosted capacity is constrained, and fall back to open models when hosted quotas are exhausted.
insights.speaker: Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Hosted and self-hosted models act as mutual capacity hedges.
